procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but the case involves an occurrence dated February 4, 1965, suggesting a trial court in Madhya Pradesh initially heard the matter.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated February 27, 1967, of the Madhya Pradesh High Court, Indore Bench in Criminal Appeals Nos. 238 and 249 of 1965.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Two criminal appeals were before the High Court, filed by two rival factions. Both sides repeated their plea of self-defense, which was rejected by the High Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants approached the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's judgment. There are two appeals before the Supreme Court: Criminal Appeal No. 83 of 1968 and Criminal Appeal No. 204 of 1967.

decision.appeal_result: Cr. A. No, 204 of 1967 allowed. Cr. A. No. 83 of 1968 dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the people of village JS had a right to use the route to the Sanwar Mosque that passed through the inimical village NS.

facts: The people of village Juna Siloda (JS) needed to travel to the Sanwar Mosque for Id prayers.
The only available route, particularly for their carts, passed through the village of Naya Siloda (NS).
The inhabitants of village NS were hostile and 'inimical' towards the people of village JS.
law: A person or group cannot be deprived of their right to use a route for a lawful purpose merely because the inhabitants of the area through which the route passes are hostile towards them.
application: The Court determined that the people of JS had a fundamental right to go to the mosque for prayers.
It reasoned that this right could not be taken away simply because the only path available went through the hostile village of NS.
The Court noted that since it was the "only cart-route," the people of JS had no alternative but to use it to return home from the mosque.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the people of village JS did have a right to use the route to the Sanwar Mosque. The Court held that the fact that the only available route passed through the inimical village of NS was not a valid reason to deprive the JS villagers of their right to travel for the lawful purpose of attending prayers.

issue.issue_text: Whether the inhabitants of village JS were justified in using force in self-defence against the inhabitants of village NS who confronted them with dangerous weapons.

facts: Inhabitants of village JS (Juna Siloda) and village NS (Naya Siloda) were rival groups with a history of animosity.
On the day of Id, the inhabitants of JS had to pass through village NS to reach the Sanwar Mosque for prayers.
After prayers, as the JS inhabitants were returning home along the same route, they were confronted by the inhabitants of NS.
The inhabitants of NS had returned from the mosque earlier, armed themselves with dangerous weapons, and were waiting on the road for the JS people.
A violent confrontation occurred, resulting in casualties on both sides.
law: Citizens have a right to use a public route, and this right is not negated by the fact that people inimical to them live along that route.
The Indian Penal Code (ss. 96-106) grants a right of private defence against unlawful aggression.
The law on self-defence is intended to encourage a spirit of self-defence and does not require a law-abiding citizen to act like a coward or run away when faced with imminent unlawful aggression.
The party that initiates the aggression (the aggressor) has no right of private defence.
application: The Court first established that the people of village JS were in the "lawful and bonafide exercise" of their right to travel to and from the mosque for prayers, even though the only route passed through the hostile village NS.

The Court identified the inhabitants of village NS as the aggressors. This was based on the finding that the NS people had returned from the mosque early, collected weapons, and deliberately waited on the road to confront the JS people.

Because the JS inhabitants were lawfully returning home and were met with an "unlawful aggression" by the armed NS group, the Court found they were "fully justified in using force in defending themselves."

The Court explicitly rejected the lower court's view that the JS people should have avoided the route to prevent a fight, stating that the law does not encourage cowardice or require citizens to abandon their rights in the face of threats.
Conversely, since the people from village NS were determined to be the aggressors, the Court held that they had no right of private defence against the people from village JS.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the inhabitants of village JS were justified in using force in self-defence because they were lawfully exercising their right to return home from the mosque when they were confronted by the inhabitants of village NS, who were the aggressors, having armed themselves and waited to attack them.

issue.issue_text: Whether the plea of self-defence raised by both sides was valid.

facts: Two rival groups of villagers, one from Juna Siloda (JS) and the other from Naya Siloda (NS), had a history of animosity.
On the day of Id, the JS group had to travel through NS to reach the Sanwar Mosque for prayers.
After prayers, the NS group returned to their village early, collected weapons, and waited on the road for the JS group to return.
When the JS group was returning along the route, they were confronted by the armed NS group, which led to a violent clash.
law: A person has a right of private defence when they are confronted with unlawful aggression while in the lawful and bona fide exercise of their own rights (such as using a public route).
The party that initiates the aggression cannot claim the right of private defence.

A person is justified in carrying arms for self-protection if they anticipate an attack while lawfully going about their business, and doing so does not negate their right to self-defence if they are attacked.
application: The Supreme Court determined that the Juna Siloda (JS) group was lawfully exercising their right to travel back to their village from the mosque using the only available route.
The Naya Siloda (NS) group, by returning early, arming themselves, and waiting on the road for the JS group, were identified as the aggressors.
Because the NS group initiated the confrontation, the JS group was justified in using force to defend themselves against this unlawful aggression.
Conversely, as the aggressors, the NS group had no right of private defence against the actions of the JS group.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the plea of self-defence was valid for the people of Juna Siloda, as they were lawfully returning to their village and were attacked by the aggressors. The plea was invalid for the people of Naya Siloda because they were the aggressors who had armed themselves and waited to confront the Juna Siloda group.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the people of village JS had a right to use the route to the Sanwar Mosque that passed through the inimical village NS.
appellant_arguments: The people of Juna Siloda (JS) had a right to use the route as it was the only one available to get to the Sanwar Mosque.
respondent_arguments: The people of Juna Siloda (JS) knew the only route was through the inimical village of Naya Siloda (NS) and therefore should have avoided using that cart track.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the inhabitants of village JS were justified in using force in self-defence against the inhabitants of village NS who confronted them with dangerous weapons.
appellant_arguments: The right of private defence was fully established, as two members of their group (Majid and Yasin) were killed before they used their weapons.
The Juna Siloda (JS) people had not gone to Sanwer with arms, whereas the Naya Siloda (NS) people had collected arms and were lying in wait for them.
They were entitled to protect themselves against the aggressive assault by the Naya Siloda (NS) people, who injured two unarmed men from the JS group when they got down from their cart.

Evidence from Naya Siloda's own witnesses showed that Latif Khan (from NS) was armed with a gun, fired first, and was only surrounded and beaten by the JS people after he had used his gun against them and exhausted his ammunition.
respondent_arguments: The Juna Siloda (JS) people should have avoided the route through Naya Siloda (NS), implying they were not justified in being there in the first place.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the plea of self-defence raised by both sides was valid.
appellant_arguments: The Juna Siloda (JS) side argued their plea was valid because they were attacked first by the Naya Siloda (NS) people who were armed and lying in wait, and they only retaliated after two of their own were killed.
respondent_arguments: The counsel for the Naya Siloda (NS) side did not put forward any serious or sustained argument that they were compelled to use force to defend themselves against unlawful aggression.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When in the lawful and bona fide exercise of a right, a person is confronted by aggressors armed with dangerous weapons, they are justified in using force in self-defense against the unlawful aggression. A person cannot be deprived of the right to use a route, and consequently the right of self-defense on that route, merely because inhabitants inimical to them are present there.
obiter: When enacting ss. 96 to l 06. l.P.C. the legislature clearly intended to arouse and encourage manly spirit Of self-defence amongst the citizens, when faced with grave danger.
The right of private defence is designed to serve a social purpose and deserves to be fostered within the prescribed Jimits.
The law does not encourage bravado.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The people of village JS had a right to use the only available route to the Sanwar Mosque, even though it passed through the inimical village NS, and could not be deprived of that right. When, in the lawful and bona fide exercise of this right, they were confronted by the inhabitants of village NS who were armed with dangerous weapons and waiting for them, the people of JS were fully justified in using force to defend themselves against this unlawful aggression.
legal_tests_applied: The right of private defence, under ss. 96 to 106 of the Indian Penal Code, is not lost simply because one is aware of a potential danger and does not avoid it. The law does not require a law-abiding citizen to behave like a coward when confronted with an imminent unlawful aggression.
An aggressor party has no right of private defence against the party they are aggressing.
why_appellant_lost: The people from village NS (appellants in Cr. A. No. 83/68) were the aggressors, and therefore, they had no right of private defence against the people from village JS.
why_respondent_won: The people of village JS (appellants in Cr. A. No. 204 of 1967) had a right to use the only route to the Mosque, and merely because the inhabitants of the village it passed through were inimical did not deprive them of that right.
The people of JS were in the lawful and bona fide exercise of their right to travel when they were confronted by the people of NS, who were armed with dangerous weapons and waiting for them.
The people of JS were justified in using force in self-defence against the unlawful aggression initiated by the people of NS.
policy_considerations: When enacting ss. 96 to 106 of the Indian Penal Code, the legislature clearly intended to arouse and encourage the manly spirit of self-defence amongst the citizens, when faced with grave danger.
The right of private defence is designed to serve a social purpose and deserves to be fostered within the prescribed limits.
The law does not require a law-abiding citizen to behave like a coward when confronted with an imminent unlawful aggression.
There is nothing more degrading to the human spirit than to run away in face of danger.
